title: HelixBank x Redwood Inference — rollback + auditability deep dive

body:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: HelixBank x Redwood Inference — rollback + auditability deep dive
Date: Jan 14, 2025
Start time: 9:00 AM PT
Duration: 58 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Dylan Brooks, Fiona McCarthy, Marcus Lin, Jada Williams
HelixBank: Renee Caldwell, Imran Qureshi, Priya Shah, Markus Vogel

Summary (auto-generated)
- HelixBank wants a controlled way to change inference “optimization configs” (batching/caching/quantization/routing knobs) with strong auditability and fast rollback.
- HelixBank’s main concern is operational risk: a config tweak can create latency spikes or errors; rollback must be one-click, safe under partial failures, and available to on-call.
- Security and compliance requirements: immutable history, evidence of who/what/where/when/why, retention controls, and export to SIEM.
- Discussion covered: config versioning model (whole-config), safe-apply with preflight validation + diff preview, canary + metric gates, rollback semantics, and RBAC.

Topics
1) Why rollback is hard for inference configs (propagation and “split brain”)
2) Safe apply workflow (preflight + diff, canary, metric gates)
3) Rollback guarantees (atomicity, idempotency, propagation status)
4) Audit logs and evidence (event taxonomy, correlation IDs, retention, redaction)
5) RBAC and approvals (who can rollback; emergency overrides)
6) Private/VPC considerations and storage location

Questions (captured)
- Can rollback be executed by SRE without broader admin rights?
- What happens if rollback is triggered while an apply is still rolling out?
- Do you log failed attempts (including denied-by-RBAC) and is that immutable?
- Can the audit log be exported to Splunk/QRadar and do you support webhook delivery?
- How do you handle secrets in configs (are they ever logged / diffed)?
- For private deployments, where is the immutable history stored and how do you handle offline/air-gapped environments?
- Can you enforce “must include ticket ID/justification” for any change?

Transcript

[00:00] Dylan Brooks: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is to go deep on rollback and auditability for optimization config changes. I know you’ve had—uh—some pain here. Renee, you want to set context from your side?

[00:15] Renee Caldwell: Yeah. Thanks Dylan. So we’re evaluating Redwood for inference serving, and we’re comfortable with the runtime story, but the operational controls are the big gating item. We’ve had incidents internally where someone changed a “performance config” and it looked fine in staging, and then prod got hammered.

[00:33] Renee Caldwell: Specifically, batching and cache toggles. Latency went up, error rate went up, and it took us longer than it should have to figure out what changed.

[00:44] Imran Qureshi: And to be blunt, we need rollback as a first-class action. Not like, “go edit a YAML and restart stuff.” We need like a button, with guardrails, and it needs to work even when things are on fire.

[00:57] Dylan Brooks: Makes sense. That’s aligned with what we’re building. The way we think about it: every optimization config change is a version. Versions are immutable. Apply is a workflow with preflight and preview, and rollback is “re-apply a known good version” with one click.

[01:14] Priya Shah: Before we get too far, I want to make sure audit logs are part of that, not an afterthought. We need a tamper-evident record of the attempt, success, failure, and who authorized it.

[01:25] Fiona McCarthy: Yep. From the security side, we treat apply and rollback as auditable events with immutable storage and export paths. We can walk through what’s in the event payload.

[01:35] Dylan Brooks: Jada’s here too—she’s been shaping the rollout workflow. Jada, want to give the 30-second overview?

[01:41] Jada Williams: Sure. In practice, “apply config” is a rollout. Even though it’s not code, it changes runtime behavior. So we model it like a deployment: preflight validation, optional canary scope, metric gates, and then full rollout with propagation tracking. Rollback is just another rollout, except the source is a prior version.

[02:05] Markus Vogel: And you said versions are immutable—so you never overwrite?

[02:10] Jada Williams: Correct. The history is append-only. You can create a new version that matches an old one, but we never mutate the old record.

[02:20] Markus Vogel: Good. We’ll need to see that for audit.

[02:24] Dylan Brooks: Let’s break it into two halves: (1) operational semantics—does rollback actually fix things fast, safely; and (2) compliance—can you prove what happened.

[02:36] Imran Qureshi: Start with semantics. Our biggest fear is partial propagation. Like config is updated in one region or one cluster and not the other and you get, like, two behaviors.

[02:47] Dylan Brooks: Yep, the “split brain” scenario.

[02:50] Imran Qureshi: Exactly.

[02:52] Dylan Brooks: So what we do is: the control plane treats apply/rollback as an atomic intent per scope. Scope can be route+model+customer+region (or a subset depending on your setup). We take a lock/lease on that scope, so only one apply is in-flight at a time.

[03:12] Jada Williams: And every apply gets an idempotency key too. So if your tooling retries because the network is flakey, you don’t accidentally start two rollouts.

[03:21] Imran Qureshi: What’s the lock duration?

[03:24] Jada Williams: Lease-based, time-bound. Default is 10 minutes with heartbeats; can be tuned. If the worker dies, lease expires, but we still have a persisted “rollout state machine” that’s recoverable.

[03:38] Renee Caldwell: Okay. But runtime-side—how does it ensure consistent application? Like, what’s the unit of rollout? Is it per pod? per node?

[03:47] Dylan Brooks: It’s per runtime instance, but orchestrated. Each instance reports “I have config version X applied.” We track convergence. If we don’t converge, we surface it as “stuck” and you can see exactly which instances are lagging.

[04:06] Imran Qureshi: And during rollback, do you stop the world? Or does traffic keep flowing?

[04:11] Jada Williams: Traffic keeps flowing. We’re not restarting processes by default. Most knobs are hot-reloadable. Some changes can require cache invalidation or warmup, and that’s flagged.

[04:23] Priya Shah: Warmup is a risk. If rollback triggers cold caches, you can create a second incident.

[04:29] Dylan Brooks: Totally. We treat a few knobs as “high risk” and we can enforce safer defaults. For example, if quantization profile changes, there’s a warmup path we recommend and we show it in the preview.

[04:42] Imran Qureshi: Quantization is one of those that scares us. Also batching. If somebody cranks batch size too high you can blow p95.

[04:51] Jada Williams: That’s why safe apply has preflight. It’s not just schema validation. It’s guardrails: bounds on batch size, constraints like “don’t enable continuous batching above X for this model family,” and compatibility checks with the selected quant profile.

[05:11] Renee Caldwell: Is that preflight customizable or is it fixed?

[05:16] Dylan Brooks: Both. There are platform defaults, and for enterprise we can allow policy overlays. Marcus can speak to how it ties into policy engine and RBAC.

[05:25] Marcus Lin: Sure. Preflight emits pass/warn/fail with structured reasons. We can enforce “fail” on certain classes, and allow override only if you have an elevated permission. The override action itself is audited.

[05:40] Priya Shah: That’s important. Overrides should be rare and visible.

[05:44] Marcus Lin: Yep. And we can require a justification string / ticket ID on any apply or rollback. It becomes a required field in the API.

[05:55] Markus Vogel: When you say ticket ID, like ServiceNow change number?

[05:58] Marcus Lin: Could be. We treat it as a generic “change_reference” field. You can standardize on “CHG1234” or “JIRA-123.”

[06:08] Renee Caldwell: Okay, good.

[06:10] Dylan Brooks: Let’s talk rollback itself. We’ve heard “one-click.” We interpret that as: from Console, choose a prior version, click rollback, confirm blast radius, and you get progress + final status.

[06:25] Imran Qureshi: What’s in the confirmation?

[06:28] Dylan Brooks: Scope, number of instances affected, and the diff summary. Like “batch.max_tokens 4096 -> 2048” and “kv_cache.enabled true -> false,” etc.

[06:41] Renee Caldwell: Diff is huge. We need to show leadership what changed.

[06:45] Dylan Brooks: We also keep metadata: author, time, source (Console/API/automation), and links.

[06:54] Priya Shah: And in the audit log, do you store the full config or the diff?

[06:59] Fiona McCarthy: We store an event with identifiers and references, plus a digest. The event includes the version IDs (from_version, to_version), scope, actor, request ID, correlation ID. We can include the diff summary as a field, but we’re careful about sensitive values.

[07:18] Priya Shah: Right, that was my next question. We can’t have secrets leaking into audit logs.

[07:23] Fiona McCarthy: Agreed. Our approach: configs should not contain secrets in the first place; secrets are referenced via secret manager integration. But regardless, the audit pipeline supports redaction rules. For example, fields marked sensitive are masked in both diff and event payload.

[07:42] Markus Vogel: Is the event log immutable in your system? Like append-only with retention policies?

[07:47] Fiona McCarthy: Yes. It’s append-only storage. Retention is configurable by tenant tier; enterprise can set longer retention. We also support export to your SIEM so you have a copy in your system of record.

[08:02] Priya Shah: Which SIEM exports are supported? We’re mostly Splunk and sometimes QRadar.

[08:08] Fiona McCarthy: Today we support webhook delivery and S3-style log export. Splunk can be either via webhook to HEC or through your collector. QRadar typically via your pipeline—webhook to your integration service.

[08:23] Priya Shah: Do you sign events? Like can we verify they’re not tampered?

[08:28] Fiona McCarthy: We can provide integrity guarantees via hashing. Internally we store a hash chain per stream; externally we include event hashes so you can detect modifications. We can share the details in the audit event spec.

[08:44] Imran Qureshi: Back to rollback in an incident: can our on-call run rollback without being full admin?

[08:51] Marcus Lin: Yes. We split permissions. Example permissions are like optimize.config.apply and optimize.config.rollback. You can grant rollback to an on-call role without granting apply, or vice versa, depending on your policy.

[09:05] Renee Caldwell: We’d probably allow rollback broadly, apply narrowly.

[09:09] Marcus Lin: That’s a common setup.

[09:12] Imran Qureshi: What about “rollback while apply is running?” That happens.

[09:17] Jada Williams: The lock prevents a second rollout on the same scope. If an apply is running and you hit rollback, the system will either (a) let you cancel the in-flight rollout if you have permission, or (b) queue rollback to start immediately after cancellation/timeout.

[09:35] Imran Qureshi: Cancel is best. But cancellation also needs to be audited.

[09:39] Fiona McCarthy: It is. Any attempted action—success, fail, denied—is logged.

[09:46] Priya Shah: Including denied-by-RBAC?

[09:48] Fiona McCarthy: Yes. The event shows actor, requested action, scope, and the denial reason class (not over-sharing). That’s important for compliance.

[10:02] Markus Vogel: What do you store as the “why”? Is it required?

[10:07] Marcus Lin: It can be required per tenant policy. If you require it, the API returns an error without it.

[10:14] Renee Caldwell: How does this work with private deployments? We may need VPC now, but there’s a chance some workloads go more isolated later.

[10:25] Dylan Brooks: For private, the same concepts, but storage is in your environment. Version history and audit logs are stored inside the private control plane database. Export to your SIEM is still possible, but it’s routed through your network.

[10:41] Priya Shah: What about air-gapped? Not sure we’re there, but we have a few regulated enclaves.

[10:47] Dylan Brooks: Air-gapped is harder. We support an on-prem package with offline operation. Audit export becomes “pull” rather than “push.” We can talk through it with our private deployments team if it gets real.

[11:04] Imran Qureshi: Let’s talk metric gates. You said canary apply with gates. What metrics? And where are thresholds set?

[11:12] Jada Williams: Default gates are p95 latency, error rate, and saturation signals. You can set thresholds at tenant level, and per environment. The canary window is configurable, like 10–30 minutes depending on volume.

[11:29] Imran Qureshi: Do you gate on quality? Like eval scores?

[11:34] Dylan Brooks: In some cases, yes, but it depends. For the initial release, quality gates are “optional” and typically based on a prompt set if you have one. Most customers start with latency + error rate.

[11:48] Renee Caldwell: For us, latency and error are the “stop the bleeding” metrics. Quality is slower to detect.

[11:54] Jada Williams: Right. And in the UI, if a gate fails, you get a clear reason and the rollback CTA is right there.

[12:06] Imran Qureshi: That’s what we want.

[12:09] Priya Shah: I want to ensure there’s traceability between config change and runtime behavior. Can you correlate config version with traces and metrics?

[12:18] Dylan Brooks: Yes. Every request is tagged with the applied config version ID at the runtime. We also include a rollout correlation ID. So you can pivot in dashboards: “after version 38, p95 jumped.”

[12:34] Priya Shah: That correlation ID—does it show up in audit logs too?

[12:38] Fiona McCarthy: Yes. Audit event includes request ID and correlation ID.

[12:43] Markus Vogel: And who can see audit logs in the Console?

[12:47] Marcus Lin: Role-based. Typically security admins and audit viewers can see the full event stream. Operators might see a summarized view. Again, configurable.

[12:59] Renee Caldwell: Let’s get concrete. Suppose we apply a config, it causes a latency spike, and we roll back. What does the timeline look like?

[13:08] Dylan Brooks: Practical goal: rollback initiated within 1–2 minutes by on-call, and convergence across instances within a few minutes. We can’t promise physics, but we can promise the workflow is fast and the state is visible.

[13:25] Imran Qureshi: “Visible” matters. Today our teams waste time guessing.

[13:29] Jada Williams: Exactly. We show per-cluster progress: pending, applying, applied, failed, stuck. If some instances fail to apply because they’re unhealthy, we show that, and you can decide whether to drain them.

[13:47] Imran Qureshi: What’s the failure mode if a subset never updates?

[13:52] Jada Williams: We mark the rollout failed or partial and we do not declare success. The system keeps retrying within bounds, and we raise alerts on stuck rollouts.

[14:04] Dylan Brooks: Also, we make apply/rollback idempotent. So a second click doesn’t create weird new versions.

[14:12] Priya Shah: I heard “whole-config rollback.” Is partial rollback possible?

[14:18] Dylan Brooks: Not in the first iteration. Whole-config rollback is simpler and safer. Partial rollback gets complicated fast—like if you revert batching but keep a quant profile. We can discuss future work, but for your risk posture, whole-config rollback is usually preferred.

[14:37] Renee Caldwell: Whole-config is fine as long as we can see diff and understand blast radius.

[14:44] Markus Vogel: Agreed. Partial rollback creates audit complexity.

[14:49] Priya Shah: One more audit thing: do you capture “source” of change? Like API vs Console vs automated system.

[14:56] Fiona McCarthy: Yes. Source is in the metadata. Also user agent / client name for API, and if it’s automation we recommend a service account.

[15:08] Marcus Lin: And service accounts are scoped with least privilege, with separate tokens and rotation policies.

[15:15] Priya Shah: Good.

[15:17] Renee Caldwell: Can you show us a sample event? Like apply_attempted.

[15:21] Fiona McCarthy: I don’t have it pasted here, but it looks like: timestamp, tenant_id, actor, action, outcome, scope, from_version, to_version, request_id, correlation_id, reason/change_reference, plus “redacted_fields” list. We’ll send a draft spec after the call.

[15:45] Imran Qureshi: Do you log the config payload itself in the version store? Because if we’re proving “what changed,” we may need full content.

[15:53] Dylan Brooks: The version store keeps the full config as a record, yes. That’s different from audit events. Audit events point to version IDs. Access to version content is permissioned. You can retrieve the config for a version if you have rights.

[16:10] Markus Vogel: That separation is good. Audit log should be low-risk but still evidentiary.

[16:16] Priya Shah: And retention on version store?

[16:19] Dylan Brooks: We support retention policies. Some customers keep “forever” within reason, but you can set retention windows and snapshot “known good” baselines.

[16:32] Imran Qureshi: Okay. Another question: if we do a rollback, does it invalidate caches? We’ve been burned by KV cache weirdness.

[16:41] Dylan Brooks: It depends on the knob. Some changes require invalidation or safe draining. The preflight and preview will flag it. We also recommend safe defaults—like if you toggle prefix cache behavior, we may do a controlled invalidation.

[16:58] Jada Williams: Also, the system can do staged rollout where canary gets the invalidation first and you observe impact.

[17:05] Imran Qureshi: That’s good.

[17:07] Renee Caldwell: Can you support “approval” workflow? Like CAB approval before apply.

[17:13] Marcus Lin: We can enforce that via required fields and permissions. Full multi-party approval is more of a workflow feature; today we integrate with your change system by requiring a ticket and optionally restricting apply to a small group.

[17:29] Markus Vogel: For emergency change, on-call can rollback without CAB, but it must be logged as emergency.

[17:35] Marcus Lin: You can encode that in the justification string or use a “change_type” field. We can discuss how we standardize that.

[17:46] Priya Shah: If you can include change_type=emergency in the audit event, that helps.

[17:50] Fiona McCarthy: Yep, we can.

[18:00] Dylan Brooks: I want to make sure we answer the “why Redwood vs X” question here. Some platforms have audit logs but not for config. We’re building it natively into Optimize config changes because it’s been a root cause of incidents.

[18:18] Renee Caldwell: We’ve looked at Bedrock and also like “roll your own” with vLLM. The issue is change control. We can do it ourselves, but it’s expensive.

[18:28] Imran Qureshi: And we’d rather not invent the wheel. But we’ll verify.

[18:33] Dylan Brooks: Totally. We’ll show the Console workflow in the next session.

[18:38] Priya Shah: In that session, I want to see: RBAC enforcement, audit log view, export configuration, and evidence of immutability.

[18:47] Fiona McCarthy: Noted.

[18:49] Dylan Brooks: We’re at time, so let’s recap next steps.

[18:54] Dylan Brooks: We’ll send: audit event taxonomy + sample payloads; RBAC permission list and example roles; and a short write-up on safe apply and rollback semantics, including lock/idempotency and propagation status.

[19:10] Renee Caldwell: And we’ll send you our internal change-management requirements and the fields we need in audit events.

[19:16] Imran Qureshi: Also our SLO targets. We want rollback MTTR under 10 minutes end-to-end.

[19:23] Jada Williams: That’s aligned with what we’re aiming for.

[19:27] Dylan Brooks: Great. We’ll schedule the Console walkthrough for early next week.

[19:33] Priya Shah: Thanks all.

[19:35] Dylan Brooks: Thanks everyone.

(End of transcript — remaining time in recording contained silence / dropped audio.)
